items.title: equals and hashCode contract
items.body: If you override equals you must override hashCode so that equal objects have equal hash codes; otherwise HashMap and HashSet look in the wrong bucket and appear to lose entries. Records generate both from their components.

items.title: Happens-before and volatile
items.body: The Java Memory Model defines happens-before: without synchronization, a write in one thread may never become visible to another or may be observed reordered. volatile guarantees visibility and ordering for that field; synchronized and Lock add mutual exclusion.
items.question: Is volatile int counter; counter++ thread-safe?
items.answer: No. counter++ is a read-modify-write; two threads can read the same value and both write back value + 1. Use AtomicInteger, LongAdder, or a lock.

source.name: Java Language Specification - Chapter 17 Threads and Locks

items.title: Virtual threads and pools
items.question: You move a blocking JDBC service to virtual threads and throughput barely improves. The connection pool has 20 connections. Why?
items.answer: Virtual threads make blocking cheap, but they do not add database capacity: at most 20 queries run at once and the rest wait for a connection. Virtual threads help when the limit is the number of platform threads, not a downstream resource. Size pools and concurrency limits (for example a Semaphore) to the real constraint.

items.title: Why Strings are immutable
items.question: Why are Java Strings immutable?
items.answer: Immutable strings can be shared across threads without locking, interned and reused, and can cache their hash code, which makes them efficient HashMap keys. Immutability also prevents a validated value such as a file path from being changed after a security check.

items.title: Mutating a key inside a HashSet
items.question: You add an object to a HashSet, then change a field used in its hashCode. contains(obj) now returns false, yet iterating the set shows it. Explain.
items.answer: The entry was stored in a bucket chosen from the old hash code. After mutation, lookups compute a new hash and search a different bucket, so the element is effectively lost for contains and remove. Use immutable keys, or remove, mutate, and re-insert.

items.title: Generational collection
items.question: Why do JVM collectors such as G1 and generational ZGC split the heap into young and old generations?
items.answer: Most objects die young. Collecting the young generation is cheap because cost scales with live objects, and survivors are promoted. Old-generation collections are rarer and more expensive, so separating them keeps pauses and CPU overhead low under high allocation rates.

source.name: Java HotSpot VM Garbage Collection Tuning Guide
